record.paper_title: On a general Syracuse problem with conjectures
record.context_brief: Cycle classification for the 3n−1 Syracuse variant
record.original_question: For the map T(n)=n/2 when n is even and T(n)=(3n−1)/2 when n is odd, are the only cycles Ω(1)=(1→1), Ω(5)=(5→7→10→5), and Ω(17)=(17→25→37→55→82→41→61→91→136→68→34→17)? Does every positive integer lie in one of the basins G(1), G(5), or G(17), so that G(∞)=∅?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 5.5. Let ν = 1 and let the parameters a = 2ν +1 = 3 and b = − 2ν +1 = − 1, then the set C(a, b ) contains exactly three cycles C(a, b ) = { Ω(1), Ω(5), Ω(17)} , and N = G(1) ∪ G(5) ∪ G(17). We have G(∞ ) = ∅ with the cycles of length 1, 3 and 11, respectively, are Ω(1) = (1 → 1), Ω(5) = (5 → 7 → 10 → 5), Ω(17) = (17 → 25 → 37 → 55 → 82 → 41 → 61 → 91 → 136 → 68 → 34 → 17).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Define the map T: ℤ⁺ → ℤ⁺ by
  T(n) = n/2     if n is even,
  T(n) = (3n−1)/2  if n is odd.
For a positive integer m, let the trajectory of m be the sequence m, T(m), T²(m), …. A cycle is a finite sequence (n₀ → n₁ → ⋯ → n_{k−1} → n₀) with T(n_i) = n_{i+1 mod k}. For a periodic point n₀, write Ω(n₀) for the cycle containing it, and let G(n₀) denote the basin of Ω(n₀), i.e. the set of all positive integers whose forward orbit under T eventually enters Ω(n₀). Let G(∞) denote the set of positive integers whose forward orbits are unbounded.

Three known cycles are:
  Ω(1) = (1 → 1),
  Ω(5) = (5 → 7 → 10 → 5),
  Ω(17) = (17 → 25 → 37 → 55 → 82 → 41 → 61 → 91 → 136 → 68 → 34 → 17).

Prove or disprove the following two statements:
(a) These are the only cycles of T on the positive integers.
(b) Every positive integer belongs to G(1) ∪ G(5) ∪ G(17); equivalently, G(∞) = ∅.
artifact.status_search_result: The 3n−1 variant of the Collatz map is a well-known open problem. It is widely conjectured that the only cycles are those rooted at 1, 5, and 17, and that no divergent trajectories exist, but no proof is known; the problem is regarded as at least as hard as the original Collatz conjecture, which itself remains unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Collatz conjecture - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The 3n−1 variant has three known cycles bottoming out at 1, 5, and 17; whether these are the only cycles is open.
status_evidence.claim: The cycles of the 3n−1 map are conjecturally exactly the ones at 1, 5, 17, and the conjecture is open.

status_evidence.title: A New 3n − 1 Conjecture Akin to Collatz Conjecture
status_evidence.snippet: Conjectures that any starting positive integer eventually reaches one of 1, 5, or 17 under the 3n−1 map.
status_evidence.claim: The statement that all positive integers fall into the basins of 1, 5, or 17 is conjectural.
